title: DevFlow AI x Redwood - onboarding feedback / first request friction
summary: DevFlow AI shared onboarding friction from a recent self-serve trial of Redwood Hosted API. Main blockers were: confusion on where to create an API key + which org/project it belongs to, docs/quickstart mismatch with current SDK methods, unclear model name selection, and lack of in-console “next step” guidance after signup. They also hit a 401 due to using a revoked key and didn’t notice the error details; wanted a clearer error surface and copyable curl/SDK snippets in the console. Team uses Node/TypeScript and Vercel; they care about low-latency streaming for an “AI pair programmer” feature and want predictable spend. Requested: onboarding checklist in console, a single minimal “first request” path, clearer rate limit/quotas visibility, and a debugging page for common errors (401/429/model not found).
topics: Signup -> API key creation flow confusion
Model selection (chat vs completions) + naming clarity
First request debugging (401/429) and surfacing error context
Desired console guidance: checklist, snippets, streaming toggle, usage dashboard
Evaluation criteria: latency, reliability, cost predictability
action_items: Redwood (Ben Carter): send DevFlow AI the minimal “hello world” snippet + recommended model for their use case (Node/TS, streaming).
Redwood (Marissa Cole): share mock of the in-console onboarding checklist and ask for feedback on step ordering (API key -> first request -> streaming -> usage dashboard).
Redwood (Jordan Blake): enable a short call next week with an SE to review their integration and confirm error handling + rate limit expectations.
DevFlow AI (Ravi Patel): retry integration using a fresh API key and confirm whether they still see a 401/429 in their staging environment.
Redwood (Nikhil Sharma): confirm current canonical base URL + SDK init pattern and flag any docs pages that are known outdated.
next_steps: Redwood to email DevFlow AI a single copy/paste first-request curl + TypeScript example (streaming) and the correct model identifier to use.
DevFlow AI to attempt first successful request again and share request/response IDs if errors persist.
Schedule 30-min technical deep dive focused on streaming + latency + rate limit guidance.

Fireflies.ai Transcript

Title: DevFlow AI x Redwood - onboarding feedback / first request friction
Date: 2026-01-22
Time: 10:03 AM - 10:36 AM (Pacific)
Duration: 33 minutes

Attendees
- Jordan Blake (Redwood)
- Ben Carter (Redwood)
- Marissa Cole (Redwood)
- Nikhil Sharma (Redwood)
- Ava Chen (DevFlow AI)
- Ravi Patel (DevFlow AI)
- Morgan Lee (DevFlow AI)

Auto-summary (generated)
- Goal: understand what blocked DevFlow AI from making a first successful request after self-serve signup.
- Key issues: API key creation discoverability, SDK/docs mismatch, model naming confusion, and error visibility.


[00:00] Jordan Blake: Cool. Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. This is Jordan from Redwood. We pulled this together mostly as, like, onboarding feedback. We saw you signed up last week, and we’d love to learn what was confusing, what was broken, and what we should fix.

[00:15] Ava Chen: Yeah, thanks. We’re happy to share. We’re trying a few providers right now, and Redwood looked promising on latency.

[00:22] Ben Carter: Hey, Ben here. I run some of the activation experiments, so I’m gonna take notes, and I may ask some annoying “where did you click” questions.

[00:30] Marissa Cole: Hi, Marissa. I’m product on the console side.

[00:34] Nikhil Sharma: Nikhil, Hosted API product. Nice to meet you all.

[00:38] Jordan Blake: Awesome. Quick context from your side would be great. What are you building and what were you trying to do when you signed up?

[00:46] Morgan Lee: I can do quick context. DevFlow AI, we’re building like an “AI pair programmer” inside our web app. It’s basically chat + tools, but the key is streaming, low-latency, and then some structured output for tasks.

[01:02] Ravi Patel: And we’re mostly TypeScript, Node, Vercel. For the LLM part we’ve tested OpenAI, Anthropic, Together, a little Bedrock via a partner. We want something that’s like fast and not insane expensive.

[01:20] Jordan Blake: Great. So what was the intended “first step” you were trying to accomplish with Redwood? Like literally, “make first request,” “get streaming working,” something else?

[01:28] Ravi Patel: The basic, make first request. Like copy/paste quickstart, get a response. We didn’t get there cleanly.

[01:35] Ben Carter: Can you walk us through what you did? Even if it’s, you know, embarrassing.

[01:40] Ravi Patel: Totally. So I signed up, got into the console. First thing I looked for was “API keys.” I saw something like “Projects” and “Organizations.” I clicked around, and I eventually found API keys but I wasn’t sure if it was per project or per org.

[01:58] Marissa Cole: Mm-hmm.

[02:00] Ravi Patel: I created a key. Then I went to docs. I clicked a Node quickstart. The snippet referenced something like `new Redwood({ apiKey })`—but when I installed the SDK the method names didn’t match exactly. Like the doc used `client.chat.completions.create` and I saw something different, or I might be mixing it with OpenAI’s SDK patterns.

[02:21] Nikhil Sharma: Got it. The SDK changed recently, so that might be a real mismatch.

[02:25] Ravi Patel: Yeah, and then model names. The docs had one model string, and in the console the model catalog showed a different naming. I tried one that looked right and got “model not found” once.

[02:39] Ben Carter: Do you remember the exact error? Like 404 or a message?

[02:42] Ravi Patel: I think it was a 404-ish. It was in the terminal, but the error object in Node was like big and we didn’t parse it. Then later we got 401.

[02:54] Jordan Blake: So you hit both model not found and then unauthorized.

[02:57] Ravi Patel: Correct.

[02:58] Ava Chen: To add: the console didn’t really tell us “do this next.” It was like, okay you’re in, now… what? We’re moving fast, so we needed a single happy path.

[03:10] Marissa Cole: That’s super helpful. When you say “do this next,” what would you want to see? Like a checklist? A big button? A modal?

[03:19] Ava Chen: A checklist is fine, honestly. Step 1: create key. Step 2: run curl. Step 3: see output. Step 4: enable streaming. Step 5: show usage. Something like that.

[03:33] Ben Carter: Yeah, and just to confirm, you did find the API keys page but it took time.

[03:37] Ravi Patel: Exactly. I found it through settings maybe. I expected it to be like right there on the homepage.

[03:44] Jordan Blake: Makes sense. On the 401, do you know what caused it? Was the key wrong, wrong header, wrong base URL, something like that?

[03:52] Ravi Patel: I think it was header + also we might have created a second key and then used the first one, or it got revoked. The console didn’t show me like “last used” or “this key is disabled” in a way I noticed.

[04:07] Marissa Cole: We do show created date, but “last used” is a good call.

[04:11] Ravi Patel: Yeah. And the other issue: base URL. The docs had one host. I googled and found another. So I wasn’t sure what the canonical endpoint is.

[04:22] Nikhil Sharma: That’s definitely something we need to clean up. There’s one canonical base URL; old docs and some blog posts used an older gateway.

[04:30] Ben Carter: This is gold. If we had to rank: what was the #1 thing that prevented first request?

[04:36] Ravi Patel: Honestly, error debugging. Like I couldn’t quickly tell if it’s me or you. The error message was not super “actionable.” If it said “401: missing header Authorization: Bearer …” I’d fix it.

[04:52] Ava Chen: +1. And the model name thing. We didn’t know which model to pick for a basic chat.

[04:59] Jordan Blake: Got it. Would it have helped if the console had a “Try it” panel where you can send a request with your key already wired?

[05:08] Morgan Lee: Yes. Like a built-in request runner. Or at least a copyable curl example with your key variable and the correct model prefilled.

[05:19] Marissa Cole: We’ve discussed an “API playground” but it’s behind. A simpler thing is we can show a snippet right after key creation.

[05:28] Ben Carter: Right, like after you click “Create API key,” next screen shows: here’s curl; here’s Node; press “Run” maybe.

[05:34] Ravi Patel: Exactly.

[05:36] Jordan Blake: Let me ask about the docs. You said mismatch with the SDK. Can you pinpoint what page or what function name mismatch?

[05:44] Ravi Patel: I don’t have it open right now. But it felt like the docs were written with an OpenAI-like interface. And I installed `@redwood/sdk`—I think that was it—and then in TypeScript, intellisense didn’t match. So I started second guessing.

[06:03] Nikhil Sharma: It might be you installed the older package name vs the new one. Or the docs point to the new one. We’ll verify.

[06:09] Ravi Patel: Could be. Also env var naming. Docs said `REDWOOD_API_KEY` but the example repo said `REDWOOD_KEY` or something.

[06:20] Ben Carter: Copy. That’s exactly the kind of paper cut we’re trying to kill.

[06:24] Ava Chen: Another thing: usage limits. We didn’t know if we were rate limited or if we were broken. Like, “do we have quota?” is a question.

[06:33] Jordan Blake: Did you hit 429?

[06:35] Ravi Patel: Not sure. Maybe once. But again we didn’t surface it nicely.

[06:40] Marissa Cole: In-console, would you expect to see rate limit and quota on the onboarding page?

[06:45] Ava Chen: Even just “you have X free credits” and “current limit: Y requests/min.” We don’t need crazy. Just enough to know what to expect.

[06:57] Jordan Blake: That makes sense.

[07:00] Ben Carter: Switching gears slightly: what made you choose Redwood to try? Was it an ad, docs, referral?

[07:06] Morgan Lee: Mostly benchmark content. Someone shared a latency chart, and we care about streaming latency. Also we saw you support dedicated later, which might matter.

[07:18] Jordan Blake: Helpful. In your ideal world, how long should it take from signup to first streamed token?

[07:24] Ravi Patel: Like 5 minutes. Ten max.

[07:28] Ben Carter: Yep, that’s the goal.

[07:31] Nikhil Sharma: On the streaming piece, were you able to test it at all?

[07:36] Ravi Patel: Not really because we didn’t get the base request stable.

[07:41] Jordan Blake: Understood. If we fix the first request path, streaming is next.

[07:46] Marissa Cole: What about console guidance beyond first request? Like once you have it working, what do you need next? Logging, dashboards, evals?

[07:55] Ava Chen: We want a usage dashboard quickly. We’ll run like a few test prompts and we want to see “how many tokens did that cost, what was the latency.” We don’t want to guess.

[08:08] Morgan Lee: Also, model versioning. Like if we test a model and later it changes, we don’t want surprises.

[08:15] Nikhil Sharma: In hosted, you can pin model versions; it’s not always obvious in the UI. Good feedback.

[08:22] Ben Carter: Another question: did you receive onboarding emails from us after signup?

[08:26] Ravi Patel: I got one, I think. But it went to promotions tab. Ava didn’t see anything.

[08:33] Ava Chen: Yeah I didn’t see it. I might have unsubscribed from something earlier, not sure.

[08:40] Ben Carter: Totally. We’re investigating deliverability right now, so that aligns.

[08:45] Jordan Blake: We can also keep it in-product so email doesn’t block onboarding.

[08:50] Ravi Patel: +1.

[08:52] Jordan Blake: I’m going to ask a more tactical question: if you had one page in the console called “Get started,” what sections should it have?

[09:00] Ava Chen: API key and endpoint, right at top. Then code snippet in the languages you support. Then a “common errors” section. Then a “see usage” link. Maybe a “what model should I use?” drop-down.

[09:16] Ravi Patel: And make the code snippet match exactly. Like if I copy it, it should run.

[09:22] Marissa Cole: Yep.

[09:24] Nikhil Sharma: For “what model should I use,” do you want it to be use-case based? Like “chat,” “embeddings,” “rerank.”

[09:31] Morgan Lee: Yes, and maybe “fast vs cheap.” Even just two choices.

[09:36] Ben Carter: That’s consistent with our messaging guidelines—latency/cost/reliability. We can simplify it.

[09:44] Jordan Blake: Any other friction points? Things like SSO, team invites, billing screens?

[09:49] Ava Chen: Billing was okay. We didn’t go far. Team invites… we didn’t even try because we weren’t activated.

[09:56] Ravi Patel: One more: when we got an error, we didn’t know if support exists. Like where do we go? Is there a “contact support” link?

[10:05] Marissa Cole: There is, but might be hidden. That’s good feedback.

[10:10] Jordan Blake: We can make that prominent during onboarding.

[10:13] Nikhil Sharma: Also, for debugging, if you share request IDs, we can look it up. Did you see request IDs in responses?

[10:21] Ravi Patel: I don’t remember seeing it. If it was in headers we didn’t print it.

[10:26] Ben Carter: That’s another thing—expose request ID in SDK errors, not just headers.

[10:31] Ravi Patel: Exactly.

[10:33] Jordan Blake: Can I ask about your evaluation criteria and timeline? Are you deciding this month?

[10:39] Ava Chen: We’re trying to pick a provider in the next 2–3 weeks. We’ll probably start with hosted and then if it works, maybe talk dedicated later.

[10:49] Jordan Blake: Okay. And what’s a “win” for you? Sub-300ms time to first token? Or consistent throughput? What matters most?

[10:58] Ravi Patel: Time to first token and streaming stability. Like no weird stalls.

[11:04] Morgan Lee: And cost predictability. We don’t need the absolute cheapest, but we need transparency.

[11:12] Nikhil Sharma: On transparency, do you want token-level breakdown or just totals?

[11:17] Morgan Lee: Totals are fine in the beginning. Later maybe details.

[11:22] Ben Carter: Makes sense.

[11:24] Jordan Blake: I’m going to rewind to the specific steps you did after signup, just so we can map it to our funnel. Do you remember: did you click “Create API key” on day one, or did you leave and come back?

[11:35] Ravi Patel: I did it day one. But I left and came back when I got stuck in the docs.

[11:41] Ben Carter: And did you ever get to the “usage” page?

[11:44] Ravi Patel: No.

[11:45] Ben Carter: Cool.

[11:47] Marissa Cole: When you created a key, did you see the key only once and then it was hidden?

[11:52] Ravi Patel: Yeah. Which is normal. But then I wasn’t sure if I saved it. I think I copied it, but I may have pasted an extra space. That could have caused 401 too.

[12:04] Nikhil Sharma: That’s possible. We can add a “test key” function.

[12:09] Ava Chen: Or show a “key is valid” check when you paste it somewhere.

[12:13] Ben Carter: In the console you can’t paste it, but in SDK we can add validation on format.

[12:19] Jordan Blake: We can do both. A simple API playground would validate it.

[12:25] Morgan Lee: Exactly.

[12:27] (crosstalk)

[12:28] Jordan Blake: Sorry go ahead.

[12:30] Ravi Patel: Another minor thing: we weren’t sure if we needed to create a “project” before keys. The UI made it feel like projects are primary.

[12:40] Marissa Cole: That’s a good point. We might be over-emphasizing projects. For self-serve, we should likely default a project and just get you running.

[12:49] Ben Carter: Yep, “create project” is an unnecessary step for activation.

[12:54] Jordan Blake: In terms of console nudges, would you find it annoying if a banner kept showing up?

[12:59] Ava Chen: If it’s dismissible and remembers, it’s fine.

[13:02] Ravi Patel: Yeah, just don’t block the page. Like a side panel or checklist card.

[13:08] Marissa Cole: Noted. We had an issue where a nudge blocked API key creation in one case; we’re fixing that.

[13:14] Ravi Patel: Yeah please don’t do that.

[13:16] Ben Carter: (laughs) agreed.

[13:18] Nikhil Sharma: On docs gaps: besides SDK mismatch, anything else? Like explanation of headers, content type, streaming format.

[13:27] Ravi Patel: Streaming format. Like is it SSE? Is it websockets? The docs said streaming but didn’t show the exact event format. We’re used to SSE chunks.

[13:38] Nikhil Sharma: It is SSE for the Hosted API. We can provide an example that prints chunks.

[13:44] Ravi Patel: Great.

[13:45] Morgan Lee: Also tool calling. We saw mention, but we didn’t know if it’s “function calling” OpenAI-style or something else.

[13:53] Nikhil Sharma: It’s similar. But we should make it consistent in docs with a single pattern.

[14:00] Ben Carter: This is super aligned with the sprint we’re running. We’re trying to reduce time-to-first-token and remove these doc mismatches.

[14:09] Jordan Blake: Let’s do this: after the call, we’ll send you a minimal curl + TypeScript snippet that we know works today, with a recommended model and streaming.

[14:18] Ravi Patel: That’d be great.

[14:20] Ava Chen: And if you have a console screenshot mock for the onboarding checklist, I’m happy to comment.

[14:26] Marissa Cole: I can share something early even if it’s rough.

[14:30] Jordan Blake: Nice.

[14:32] Ben Carter: One more question on attribution. You said promotions tab. Would you prefer in-console messages over email? Like, if we do both, is that okay?

[14:41] Ava Chen: Both is okay, but console should be primary.

[14:45] Ravi Patel: Yep.

[14:47] Jordan Blake: Cool.

[14:49] Nikhil Sharma: For the immediate unblock, if you want, we can stay on the line and debug one of the requests live. But I know we only scheduled 30.

[14:58] Ravi Patel: I don’t have the repo ready right now. But I can try again after you send the snippet.

[15:04] Jordan Blake: Perfect.

[15:06] Marissa Cole: Can I ask: do you prefer the onboarding page to link to docs, or should it embed everything? Like code snippets in-console.

[15:14] Ava Chen: Embed the basics. Link to docs for details.

[15:18] Morgan Lee: Yeah, keep it minimal.

[15:20] Ben Carter: Minimal is key. One “happy path.”

[15:24] Jordan Blake: Anything else we didn’t cover? Competitors you’re leaning toward or anything that Redwood must have?

[15:31] Ava Chen: Honestly, OpenAI is easiest. But we’re worried about cost and some policy stuff. Anthropic is good but also cost. Together is closer to what we want but we’ve seen variability. We want stability.

[15:46] Jordan Blake: Totally. Redwood’s pitch is stable performance and good economics. We’ll make sure onboarding doesn’t get in your way.

[15:55] Nikhil Sharma: Also, once you’re through onboarding, we can share how to pin model versions and set fallback policies. That’s a reliability lever.

[16:03] Morgan Lee: Cool.

[16:05] Ben Carter: Quick check: if we fix the first request and streaming examples, would you continue evaluating Redwood?

[16:11] Ava Chen: Yes. That’s literally the blocker.

[16:14] Ravi Patel: Yep.

[16:16] Jordan Blake: Great. Let me recap next steps and then we’ll let you go.

[16:20] Jordan Blake: Redwood side: Ben will send the minimal “hello world” snippet in TypeScript plus curl, and the correct model identifier for chat + streaming. Marissa will share a rough mock of an in-console onboarding checklist so you can react. I’ll set up a 30-minute technical follow-up next week in case you hit errors again.

[16:37] Jordan Blake: DevFlow side: Ravi, if you can retry with a fresh key and let us know if you still get 401 or “model not found” or 429, and if possible share the request IDs or timestamps, we’ll dig in.

[16:49] Ravi Patel: Sounds good.

[16:51] Ava Chen: Works.

[16:53] Morgan Lee: Thank you.

[16:55] Jordan Blake: Thanks all. Appreciate the candid feedback—this is exactly what we need.

[17:01] (Call ends)
